tldr: This is a loose cluster around a shared label, not one developing event. Late October brought two Show HN agent tools calling themselves control planes, flightdeck for observability and Omneum for local context management, and on Nov 4 the vLLM blog introduced Kinference, an open source inference control plane for vLLM on Kubernetes.
whats_new: GitSeed, posted to Hacker News on Nov 15, applies the label to coding agents: a self-hosted control plane for running AI coding agents.
why_it_matters: "Control plane" now names three different layers: agent observability, coding-agent orchestration, and multi-tenant inference serving. Check which layer a tool actually governs before adopting it.

beats.headline: Two Show HN projects pitch control planes for AI agents
beats.summary: flightdeck targets observability and control of running agents; Omneum targets local, text-blind context management.

beats.headline: Kinference brings an open source control plane to vLLM on Kubernetes
beats.summary: Token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, and load balancing for self-run inference platforms.

beats.headline: GitSeed pitches a self-hosted control plane for coding agents
beats.summary: The label returns to open source agent tooling, scoped to AI coding agents.

open_questions: Does Kinference see adoption or contributions beyond its launch post on the vLLM blog?
Do flightdeck or Omneum gain users or contributors after their Show HN posts?
What does GitSeed actually control for coding agents: sandboxes, permissions, repo access, or just job scheduling?
take_for_builders: If you run vLLM on Kubernetes, evaluate Kinference for per-tenant rate limits and cost tracking in a staging cluster. Treat GitSeed, flightdeck and Omneum as early experiments until they show releases and outside contributors.
